chapter: Las Vegas, Sinatra and later years
title: The Parker-Gillespie session: 'Congo Blues'
summary: A Cleveland man pressed him to record; he assembled Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Flip Phillips, Teddy Wilson and others for a 12-inch date, and 'Congo Blues' was voted record of the year.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: That's right. Let's hold on a minute. Red, we've got just a little bit of time left here. And I never did with -- I mean you've been recording for years and years, I just turn up the book and there's pages of it. We -- although you talk about one or two things you did, we never really did go onto the subject of all of the records that you made. And I mean some of those sessions were outstanding. You didn't say anything about the session you made where you had Charlie Parker, you had Dizzy, can you remember those sessions? Or should I --
Can I remember them?
Well, I mean, do you remember the session I'm talking about?

Yeah, I remember the sessions very well. Well at the time I think I was in that time I was with Benny or during it, just before, and one morning a fella called me about 8:00 clock and said, "I'd like for you to do a record today." I said, "No, I've recorded too much, I don't want to do a record date." So, he said, "I'm in from Cleveland and I wanted -- I came expressly to talk to you about doing something." And I said, "Well, I'm recording with different ones and I really don't want to be leader on a date like this. Or that date." So, then we kept talking and -- a little bit and I finally said, I really want to get rid of him ready, so I said, "If you'll let me do what I want to do, pay me so much, let me

get the men I want, let me pay them what I want, I'll do a date for you. // And he said, 'All right, I'll let you know.' So I forgot about it, really. The next day I hadn't thought anymore about it. About two weeks later he called me back says okay on that date. I says, 'What date?' So he explained who he was and I said okay.

So we got going and I had known Charlie Parker in Kansas City, course I knew Dizzy in New York, and Flip and Ralph Burns had worked with me in a small band. And course I knew Teddy and all. I just -- the idea hit me to get these -- get these people together for the date. And we started at 9:00 in the morning. That's it. We had no music, no nothing, and it just seemed to jell. Everybody seemed to jell.

And, actually it was a nervewracking date forme because it was a 12-inch instead of a 10-inch, I didn't realize, but after he said okay to these things, he said the 12-inch. And I guess on account the money he was spending. But, and it was still not taped in those days, so a lot of times, mistakes were made, we had to go back and correct them and lose the --
What were some of the titles?
But it was a good date --
What were some of the titles?
Oh, 'Congo Blues', 'Get Happy', 'Hallelujah',
" Slam Slam Blues, " those were the four sides I made.
Yeah.
And " Congo Blues " was voted the record of the year, that next year.
Yeah, that's good Red, that's -- we're going to run out of tape, here I see, but really that's what we -- that was one outstanding session, wasn't it?
Well I think it was a date where people were possibly different but they were -- but it was putting it together in such a way that they're very fraternally good on this --
Yeah.
I don't know what it is -- everything went --
Didn't you say that you saw Charlie on the Street and he said, " How about that session? "

Oh, yes, he said, " How about that record, it's got the prize -- this year, I say, " What can I do, " he said, " Get me in to hear Benny Goodman, " I was working with Benny at the 500, I says, " You got it. " So he came in, he enjoyed it. He enjoyed hearing Benny.
That was a twist, wasn't it?
Yeah.
